back: The share of context tokens that help the task; noise costs money and quality even when the window is not full.
Many models use information at the start and end of a long context more reliably than in the middle; verify on your model.
Standing rules first, evidence and the question last; repeat a critical middle fact near the end.

front: Truncate vs summarise vs structured memory
back: Truncation loses silently; summaries are lossy and can hallucinate; structured memory needs a schema but keeps durable facts.
Rewriting history every turn changes the prefix and breaks prefix caching; compact when a budget is exceeded.
Retrieval: cheap, focused, can miss. Long context: no retrieval miss, expensive, weak middle; fits bounded document sets.
Only a prefix is cached: the first differing token ends the match.
System, tools, examples, reused documents, history up to the last turn, then the new user message.
A write costs w times the base price, a read r times (e.g. 1.25 and 0.1 in the source's explicit-marker scheme; check current prices).

front: Average cost of 1 write + n reads
back: $(w+rn)/(n+1)$ relative to no caching; pays back when $n>(w-1)/(1-r)$.
Changing early tokens (timestamps, ids), reordered tools, TTL expiry between requests, prefix below the minimum size.
Exact: hash of the full prompt, safe at temperature 0. Semantic: embedding similarity threshold; risk of similar-but-different questions.
Check cache-read token counts in the usage fields; alert when they are zero.
